thread.title: Here are the risks stock-market bulls should fear most in 2019: HSBC - MarketWatch

author: Barbara Kollmeyer
title: Here are the risks stock-market bulls should fear most in 2019: HSBC - MarketWatch
text:
If this not-so-horrible week keeps up, the S&P 500 could be in line for a nice weekly win, after that grim start to the month.
Thank that everything-is-awesome attitude on the trade front for any gains we’re getting. Still, look beyond December and there’s plenty of caution. As this column’s call pointed out Wednesday, a too-quiet 2017 hardly prepared us for 2018’s battering and volatility whirl-a-gig.
Forewarned is forearmed and our call of the day from strategists at HSBC offer up the biggest risks they see facing markets next year.
1) Corporate margins stumble and fall. “A meaningful decline in profit margins — perhaps driven by an acceleration in wage growth — could be enough to derail forecast U.S. profits growth, and hence the U.S. bull market – especially if resurgent wages saw the Fed driven to tighten monetary policy further,” said HSBC global equity strategist Ben Laidler and team. That would also mean companies could be in trouble where borrowing is concerned.
2) Fed keeps hiking. HSBC sees two more hikes after one at next week’s meeting—March 2019 and June 2019, but markets are warming up to the idea the central bank may have to pare those plans. Strong growth and higher inflation could mean the Fed gets aggressive.
This could work two ways for stocks. If the Fed is responding to higher inflation spurred by stronger growth, then stocks could rise, but if that tightening is a response to tariff-related inflationary pressure, equities could get hit. In this case, opt for defensive stocks, says HSBC.
3) Rising borrowing costs for companies. “If corporates were to be faced with the combined challenge of the increased cost of borrowing, and potentially lower operating profits in an economic downturn, then it is likely that some would struggle,” said HSBC. Their biggest worry is the “degraded credit profile of U.S. dollar based investment grade nonfinancial companies.
4) The return of fixed-income volatility. It’s been low for the last several years, but signs of more Fed tightening and a possible start of higher rates from Europe’s central bank next year could start shake things up. “As a result, it seems likely that higher fixed income vols would spill over into other asset classes. an increase in equity vol would be associated with equities selling off.”
Volatility wave keeps rolling HSBC tossed in other risks that could hit an array of assets — rising climate-change costs, a trade war gets settled (good, but could also trigger tighter Fed policy), another eurozone crisis, new and unconventional ECB policies and surprise reforms by emerging-market countries.

The market The S&P SPX, +0.03% Dow DJIA, +0.29% and Nasdaq COMP, -0.22% have all opened modestly higher.
Crude US:CLU8 is lower after an IEA report showed rising OPEC production , while the dollar DXY, +0.18% and gold US:GCU8 are steady. Watch the euro EURUSD, -0.1319% as the ECB meets later and the pound GBPUSD, +0.0475% for more Brexit developments and after PM Theresa May won her confidence vote.
Europe stocks SXXP, -0.13% are slipping, while Asia stocks rallied for a second day, with China stocks SHCOMP, +1.23% up 1.3% .
The chart So while November was a mess for stocks, that didn’t stop investors from pouring money into the SPDR S&P 500 ETF SPY, +0.07% which tracks the index. It scooped up another $3.73 billion for November, the most flows for any ETF in that month, according to ETFGI.com . The buzz GE GE, +8.79% is flying on news that it will launch an independent, $1.2 billion industrial internet-of-things software company and after an upgrade by J.P. Morgan .
Apple AAPL, +1.50% is putting $1 billion into a new Austin campus , and plans to expand across other cities. Apple says this is part of its plans to add 20,000 new jobs in the U.S. by 2023.
While the trade tensions between the U.S. and China may be easing a bit, relations may be souring elsewhere as a second Canadian ex-diplomat may have gone missing in China . Some are concerned it may amount to retailing over Canada arresting a high-profile Huawei executive at the behest of the U.S. Justice Department.
In Europe, the European Central Bank says it’s bond-buying program will officially end this year, and left key interest rates unchanged. UCG, +1.37% And after surviving the night of long knives, May is in Brussels to fight for a better Brexit deal.

“And 13 times out of those 36 years the S&P actually finished the year with positive double-digit returns (as happened in 2009, 2010 and 2016),” writes Carlson .
